Fireflies.ai Transcript Export

Title: Acme Fintech Security Review — Optimize Guardrails + Audit Logs
Date: 2025-01-14
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees
- Miguel Santos (Redwood Inference)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference)
- Ethan Park (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (Acme Fintech)
- Mark Ellison (Acme Fintech)
- Elena Petrova (Acme Fintech)
- Jordan Kim (Acme Fintech)

Summary (auto-generated)
Acme asked detailed questions about Redwood’s new “Optimize guardrails gating” feature, specifically around audit logging for configuration changes, retention of audit records and evaluation artifacts, and who can override a failed or timed-out gating check. Redwood described the control-plane enforcement point, audit event structure, RBAC restrictions and “break glass” workflow, and typical retention defaults with configurable options for enterprise tiers. Acme also asked about export to SIEM, data residency, and whether prompts/outputs are stored as part of eval artifacts.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Audit logs: schema, fields, immutability, export
2) Gating outcomes: pass/fail/timeout and how recorded
3) Overrides: who can do it, approval, rate limits
4) Retention: eval artifacts vs audit records, customer configuration
5) Security posture: encryption, key management, data access

Questions (auto-generated)
- Do you log the exact config delta and who initiated it?
- If someone overrides, is that a separate event and does it require a second approver?
- How long do you retain eval runs, prompt sets, and artifacts? Can we set it to 1 year?
- Can we export to Splunk and prove to auditors the guardrails ran before changes?

Transcript

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Cool, thanks everyone. Um, this is the security and compliance review on the guardrails and audit logs piece. I’m Miguel, I run the account on our side. I’ve got Naomi from security requirements, Kevin for audit log export / SIEM stuff, Marcus for security architecture, and Ethan who owns the control plane enforcement, so the “where does gating happen” question.

[00:22] Priya Desai: Great. Yeah, thanks. We’re evaluating Redwood for inference and also the Optimize feature, but we have strict change management. We had a prior vendor where “optimization” basically meant quality drift and no evidence trail.

[00:35] Miguel Santos: Yep, understood.

[00:37] Priya Desai: So the core is: when Optimize applies batching, caching, quantization, routing tweaks, whatever—can we prove to an auditor that an evaluation ran and passed before the change went live? And, who can override, and how is that controlled.

[00:57] Ethan Park: I can start with “where it’s enforced.” The gating is enforced in the control plane at the point we apply an Optimize proposal. So whether you do it via Console or API, it’s the same endpoint and the same policy evaluation. We don’t rely on the UI for enforcement.

[01:15] Elena Petrova: Control plane meaning… separate from the runtime cluster?

[01:19] Ethan Park: Correct. Runtime is serving, but the change application and policy enforcement is upstream. That gives us auditability and consistency across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

[01:31] Mark Ellison: Okay. So if someone hits the API directly, they still get blocked if evals fail.

[01:35] Ethan Park: Exactly. Unless they have explicit override permissions, which Naomi can explain.

[01:42] Naomi Feldman: Yep. The override path is not a “click through.” It’s RBAC gated and we recommend a two-step process for enterprise. In our standard model, override is limited to specific roles—like “Org Admin” or a custom “Guardrails Override Approver.” And we capture a justification string and optionally a ticket link.

[02:04] Priya Desai: Is that optional or mandatory? Justification.

[02:06] Naomi Feldman: Mandatory for override. For regular applies, you still get who/what/when, but justification is only required when you’re bypassing a block.

[02:17] Jordan Kim: And that’s logged, presumably.

[02:19] Kevin Osei: Yes. Override is logged as its own event, plus it’s linked to the original gating run. So you can see “Apply attempted → gating failed or timed out → override requested → override approved → config applied.”

[02:37] Mark Ellison: Can you talk specifics on the audit event? Like fields. We need actor, source IP, before/after.

[02:46] Kevin Osei: Sure. High level, the audit event for Optimize config change includes: tenant/org ID, environment, the actor identity (user or service principal), auth method, timestamp, request ID, and then the config delta—like “quant_profile: fp16 → int8” or “batching.max_batch_tokens: 2048 → 4096.” Also it includes the gating evaluation metadata: eval suite name(s), suite version, prompt-set revision ID, model version(s) tested, and the outcomes per metric.

[03:20] Priya Desai: “Outcomes per metric” meaning you store scores.

[03:24] Kevin Osei: We store aggregated results in the audit event at a summary level—pass/fail, and the relevant deltas and thresholds that drove the decision. The full eval artifact is separate storage with its own retention controls.

[03:39] Mark Ellison: Right, because we don’t want prompts or generated outputs in audit logs if they might contain sensitive content.

[03:46] Marcus Lin: Exactly. Audit logs are intentionally minimal and structured, and we have redaction rules. The eval artifacts can contain prompt text depending on how you run the eval harness. For regulated customers, we support “no prompt retention” mode where you store only hashes or IDs and keep the actual prompts in your system.

[04:10] Elena Petrova: Wait, so where do prompt sets live? In Redwood or in our bucket?

[04:15] Ethan Park: Both options. By default, for hosted customers, prompt sets used for gating can be uploaded to Redwood with access controls. For more sensitive cases, we can reference prompt sets stored in your environment and run evals in a private deployment, or we can accept prompt payloads per run without storing them.

[04:35] Priya Desai: I’m going to be blunt: do you store our prompts and outputs by default?

[04:42] Miguel Santos: For production inference, no—by default we don’t store request/response bodies beyond transient processing, unless you enable logging features. For eval runs, the default depends on the eval runner configuration. Our enterprise recommendation is: store summaries + metrics, store artifacts for a short time (like 14 or 30 days) for debugging, and keep long-term evidence in audit logs and exports.

[05:08] Priya Desai: Okay. We need a written statement on that. But continue.

[05:13] Mark Ellison: On retention. What are your defaults and what’s configurable?

[05:18] Kevin Osei: Typical defaults we’re aligning to: audit logs retained 1 year for enterprise tiers (can be longer), eval artifacts retained 30 days by default. You can configure artifact retention down to like 7 days or disable, depending on deployment. For private deployments, you control the underlying storage retention.

[05:40] Jordan Kim: If we request 7 years for audit logs, is that a thing?

[05:45] Kevin Osei: It can be, but we usually do that via export to your SIEM or your archive storage. Keeping 7 years inside the product is possible on some plans, but SIEM export is the standard. We can discuss contractually.

[06:03] Priya Desai: For us it’s typically: product keeps 400 days, SIEM keeps 7 years.

[06:08] Kevin Osei: That’s consistent.

[06:10] Mark Ellison: Export method. Is it pull API, push webhook, or like S3 delivery?

[06:16] Kevin Osei: Today we have a pull API for audit events, and for enterprise we can enable near-real-time delivery via webhook. S3 delivery is on the roadmap; some customers do “pull to collector” and forward to Splunk.

[06:34] Priya Desai: We’re Splunk. We need something deterministic and complete, not sampling.

[06:39] Kevin Osei: Audit logs are not sampled. Metrics might be sampled; audit events are not.

[06:45] Elena Petrova: And include who did it. We need service accounts too.

[06:49] Kevin Osei: Yep. Service principals show as a separate actor type; you can restrict them via RBAC. We also include “acting on behalf of” if it’s via an automation tool.

[07:02] Mark Ellison: Can an engineer create a service principal with override permission and bypass?

[07:08] Naomi Feldman: Not without admin privileges. Override permission is a distinct capability. In SSO/SAML environments, you map it to a group. Also, we recommend that override actions require MFA and, optionally, a second approver.

[07:23] Priya Desai: You said “optionally.” Is second approval implemented or is that a process doc.

[07:28] Naomi Feldman: It’s partially product, partially process. Product-wise, we can require an “approver” field distinct from “requestor” for override in enterprise mode, and we enforce that they’re different identities. Some customers still route it through their internal ticketing for approvals, but the system can enforce two-person.

[07:52] Mark Ellison: Nice. And do you rate limit overrides? Like, someone can’t just override everything for a week.

[07:58] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we have per-tenant rate limits and we can set policy like “max N overrides per day” or “override only allowed for certain optimization types.” Quantization overrides are more restricted in many setups.

[08:12] Ethan Park: And you can scope overrides by route or environment. For example, allow override only in staging, or only for a specific model family.

[08:22] Elena Petrova: Speaking of environments, do you distinguish staging/prod in audit logs?

[08:26] Kevin Osei: Yes. Environment is a field, along with region.

[08:31] Priya Desai: Okay. Now, on gating outcomes. If a gating eval times out, do you log that? And what happens? Because timeouts happen.

[08:42] Ethan Park: We log timeouts. In terms of behavior: it’s policy-based. For higher tiers, we default to “blocked” if the eval runner can’t produce a decision in time. Some customers choose “manual approval required” which is basically override workflow. We generally do not default to “allow on timeout” for production.

[09:06] Mark Ellison: Good.

[09:07] Priya Desai: So there’s a safe-fail closed.

[09:10] Ethan Park: Correct. Fail closed.

[09:12] Elena Petrova: But does that mean an outage of the eval runner blocks all config changes?

[09:18] Ethan Park: Yes for gated changes, unless your policy says “manual approval.” There’s also an “observe-only” mode during rollout where we log results but don’t enforce.

[09:31] Miguel Santos: That’s part of the rollout plan—observe-only, then soft block, then hard block.

[09:38] Priya Desai: We’d want hard block for prod.

[09:41] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[09:43] Mark Ellison: How do you ensure the gating decision is tied to the exact config delta applied? Like, no TOCTOU issues.

[09:51] Ethan Park: Great question. The eval run is keyed on the exact proposed change: model version, prompt set revision, suite, and the config delta. When you apply, the control plane verifies the gating run corresponds to the same inputs. If anything differs, it requires a new eval.

[10:11] Mark Ellison: And that linkage is in the audit log.

[10:14] Kevin Osei: Yep, it’s in the event: gating_run_id and the hashes/identifiers.

[10:19] Priya Desai: You said “hashes.” Is that like a hash of the prompt set.

[10:23] Ethan Park: Prompt-set revision ID plus a content hash in some modes, yes.

[10:29] Marcus Lin: The core idea is non-repudiation: you can’t claim “we ran evals” if it was for a different suite or different model build.

[10:39] Priya Desai: That’s exactly what we need.

[10:42] Jordan Kim: I want to ask on scope—does this apply to model upgrades too or only config changes.

[10:49] Miguel Santos: Today the project is focused on Optimize-driven config changes. Model upgrades can be gated too, but it’s not the first deliverable. That said, model version pinning is part of the metadata.

[11:03] Priya Desai: Okay.

[11:05] Mark Ellison: Another question: do audit logs include the exact threshold numbers? Like “must not regress > 1.5 points.”

[11:13] Kevin Osei: Yes, at least for the metrics that triggered the decision. For example: “format compliance >= 0.98, observed 0.965, fail” or “toxicity <= 0.02, observed 0.015, pass.” We do not include raw per-prompt results in the audit log.

[11:34] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[11:35] Elena Petrova: How do you calculate those, like confidence intervals? Sorry, I’m mixing. But we don’t want flappy decisions.

[11:43] Ethan Park: The eval harness outputs aggregated metrics plus confidence intervals where applicable. The policy engine uses minimum sample sizes and can do “must be within CI” type rules. The audit log includes whether the decision used CI or fixed delta. I think Kevin said “thresholds,” but it can also log “min_samples=200 met.”

[12:08] Mark Ellison: Good.

[12:10] Priya Desai: Let’s talk access to audit logs. Are they immutable, and who can view them.

[12:16] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs are append-only. No one can edit or delete individual events. Access is via RBAC, and we recommend restricting “view audit logs” to security and admins. We also support export so you have an external system of record.

[12:36] Mark Ellison: Are Redwood employees able to see our audit logs.

[12:40] Marcus Lin: By default, no, not unless you grant support access, and even then it’s controlled. For enterprise we can do support access with explicit customer approval, time-bounded. In private deployment, you can keep logs entirely in your environment.

[12:57] Priya Desai: Okay. Encryption at rest, KMS.

[13:01] Marcus Lin: Standard: encryption in transit TLS, encryption at rest, and for private you can integrate KMS/HSM. In hosted, we have a managed KMS; for dedicated tiers we can discuss customer-managed keys in some setups.

[13:17] Mark Ellison: Data residency. Where are eval artifacts stored.

[13:21] Marcus Lin: Region-scoped. If your deployment is in US-West, artifacts are in that region. We can also pin to EU region if that’s where the tenant is.

[13:33] Elena Petrova: The gating eval runner traffic—does it hit production GPUs? We don’t want evals messing with customer workloads.

[13:41] Ethan Park: We isolate eval jobs; they can run on separate capacity pools. We also throttle concurrency. It depends on tier and configuration. But yes, we treat them separately from serving traffic.

[13:57] Priya Desai: Ok.

[14:00] Mark Ellison: On the override workflow: can you walk an example. If gating fails, what does the user see, and what gets logged.

[14:09] Miguel Santos: Sure. In Console, they’d see “Apply blocked: quality checks failed.” There’s a panel with the metrics and the reason. They can click “Request override” if they have permission to request. If they don’t, they can’t proceed.

[14:23] Naomi Feldman: And in API, it returns a structured error with failure reasons and gating_run_id. If override is allowed, there’s a separate endpoint to submit override justification.

[14:36] Mark Ellison: Does “request” mean someone else approves.

[14:39] Naomi Feldman: In enterprise mode, yes, you can require second approver. Otherwise, if the same person has both capabilities, they can override directly, but we advise against that.

[14:50] Priya Desai: We would require second approver for production. Probably security group.

[14:55] Naomi Feldman: That’s common.

[14:57] Kevin Osei: Audit-wise, you get at least two events: override_requested and override_approved (or denied), plus the eventual config applied event. All linked.

[15:10] Jordan Kim: Is there any “break glass” if something is on fire and gating is blocking.

[15:16] Ethan Park: Break-glass is essentially override with higher privilege and stricter auditing. You can create a role that is normally empty and only temporarily assigned. When used, it’s very visible in logs and can trigger alerts.

[15:33] Priya Desai: Can we alert on override usage.

[15:36] Kevin Osei: Yes. We have webhook integrations and dashboards; we can also send notifications on override events. Many customers send it to Slack or PagerDuty, and to SIEM.

[15:49] Mark Ellison: Great.

[15:51] Priya Desai: Another area: what do you log about the gating itself? Like, if there’s a new prompt set version, does that show.

[15:59] Ethan Park: Yes, prompt-set revision is recorded. If prompt set changes, previous gating runs are not valid for new changes; and the log will reflect the revision.

[16:12] Elena Petrova: And what about model version. We run multiple model versions sometimes.

[16:18] Ethan Park: Model version (or build hash) is recorded. If the model changes under the hood, you need a re-eval. We treat that as invalidation.

[16:28] Mark Ellison: That helps.

[16:31] Priya Desai: Okay, now a tricky one: We require minimal PII exposure. If someone submits prompt sets for eval, do you have scanning or classification.

[16:44] Marcus Lin: We don’t automatically classify your prompts as PII or not, but we provide guidance and tooling to avoid uploading sensitive data. For regulated workflows, we strongly recommend synthetic or redacted prompt sets, or running evals in your VPC/private deployment.

[17:03] Priya Desai: So no automatic DLP.

[17:06] Marcus Lin: Not as a default feature today.

[17:08] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:10] Mark Ellison: On “private deployment,” is the audit log the same schema.

[17:14] Ethan Park: Same schema. It’s generated by the control plane components. In private, you host it; you can export to your systems.

[17:25] Elena Petrova: What about on-prem.

[17:28] Miguel Santos: For on-prem, same idea. We may have differences depending on your storage, but the event schema is consistent.

[17:36] Jordan Kim: I’m going to ask a procurement-ish thing: does this audit log export cost extra.

[17:42] Miguel Santos: For enterprise tiers, export is typically included. We can confirm in pricing. Some advanced retention or custom export may be an add-on.

[17:53] Priya Desai: Okay. Another question: are you SOC 2, ISO.

[17:57] Marcus Lin: Yes, SOC 2 Type II. ISO 27001 is in progress—depending on timing. We can share reports under NDA.

[18:08] Priya Desai: Great.

[18:10] Mark Ellison: Let’s dig into a possible failure mode. Suppose an optimization is applied, later we find quality regressed. Do you have rollback and is that logged.

[18:20] Ethan Park: Rollback exists as a control-plane action as well. It’s logged as another config change, with “rollback_of_event_id” reference. And we can attach the reason.

[18:33] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[18:35] Elena Petrova: And if the eval runner is down, you said blocked. But can we set, like, “allow only in staging” or “allow for dedicated only.”

[18:46] Ethan Park: Yes. Policies can vary by tenant tier and environment. Most enterprise will block in prod, allow in staging, and require manual approval in prod if runner is degraded.

[19:01] Mark Ellison: How do you determine degraded.

[19:03] Ethan Park: Timeouts, error rates, job backlog—SRE signals. But from policy perspective, it’s “no gating result within X minutes” yields timeout.

[19:14] Priya Desai: Good. We also care about determinism. If you re-run the same eval, do you get same decision.

[19:21] Ethan Park: We’re working to make it deterministic as possible. The outputs are aggregated and sorted. But model inference has some nondeterminism; we mitigate with fixed seeds where possible and use statistical thresholds.

[19:36] Mark Ellison: Okay, so it’s not bit-identical but policy stable.

[19:40] Ethan Park: Exactly.

[19:42] Priya Desai: If you do “observe-only” first, is that logged the same.

[19:47] Kevin Osei: Yes, the gating run is logged, and the apply event indicates enforcement mode: observe-only, soft-block, hard-block.

[19:59] Priya Desai: That’s useful.

[20:01] Jordan Kim: Does soft-block mean they can continue anyway.

[20:05] Naomi Feldman: Soft-block typically means UI warns and requires an explicit acknowledgement or an override depending on configuration. For some tenants, soft-block is basically “override recommended but not required.” For yours, it sounds like you’d want hard-block in prod.

[20:24] Priya Desai: Yes.

[20:25] Mark Ellison: I want to go back to “config delta” in the audit event. Is it the full config or just diff.

[20:32] Kevin Osei: Both are possible. Usually we log a normalized diff to keep payload sizes reasonable. We also store a snapshot reference ID if you need the full before/after config, but again we avoid huge payloads.

[20:49] Mark Ellison: Okay.

[20:51] Elena Petrova: Is the “routing tweak” considered config too.

[20:55] Ethan Park: Yes. Anything that changes routing policy is part of configuration state, so it’s logged.

[21:01] Priya Desai: If Optimize suggests something but we don’t apply, is there an event.

[21:06] Miguel Santos: Not always. Proposals can be viewed; viewing isn’t necessarily audited unless you enable that. Applying is audited.

[21:15] Priya Desai: Fine.

[21:17] Mark Ellison: Can we get an example event. Like a redacted sample.

[21:21] Kevin Osei: Yes, we can provide a sample JSON. It’ll have fields like event_type=OptimizeConfigChangeApplied, gating_decision=pass/fail/timeout, override=true/false, override_justification, suite_id, prompt_set_rev.

[21:39] Priya Desai: Great. We’ll need that for internal review.

[21:44] Miguel Santos: We’ll send it.

[21:46] Priya Desai: Competitors wise, we’re comparing to Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. They both have some audit logging but it’s not specific to “quality gating.” So the unique piece is you’re asserting quality checks.

[22:00] Miguel Santos: Correct. We’re trying to make “cost optimization” safe by default.

[22:04] Elena Petrova: On the metrics, do you log what metrics you used.

[22:08] Ethan Park: Yes, metric names are logged. Like “task_success,” “format_compliance,” “toxicity,” maybe “factuality_proxy.” It’s configurable by workload.

[22:24] Mark Ellison: And those names are stable? We don’t want you renaming stuff and breaking our SIEM parsing.

[22:31] Kevin Osei: We version the schema. Changes are backwards compatible or versioned, and we give release notes.

[22:38] Priya Desai: Okay.

[22:40] Marcus Lin: Also to clarify, we can provide a schema registry doc—field definitions and types.

[22:47] Priya Desai: Good.

[22:49] Mark Ellison: On RBAC, do you integrate with SAML.

[22:52] Naomi Feldman: Yes. SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning. You can map groups to roles.

[23:00] Priya Desai: Great.

[23:02] Elena Petrova: One more. Does Redwood staff ever use override on our behalf.

[23:09] Naomi Feldman: No by default. If you explicitly request support to do an operation, it’s possible only with your approval and it would show the actor as a Redwood support identity with “support session” metadata. But we try not to do that, and for private deployment it’s not possible without you granting access.

[23:28] Priya Desai: Okay.

[23:30] Mark Ellison: Let’s talk about “immutability.” If I export to Splunk, fine. But inside Redwood, can an org admin delete audit logs.

[23:39] Kevin Osei: No. They can’t delete individual audit events. Retention policies can be changed prospectively, but you can’t go back and erase. And exports are recommended.

[23:53] Priya Desai: That’s important.

[23:55] Jordan Kim: Okay. I think we’ve hit the big topics.

[23:59] Priya Desai: I have one last thing: evidence. We need to demonstrate to auditors that for every change, there exists a corresponding evaluation run. Can we run a report.

[24:11] Kevin Osei: Yes. You can query audit events for config changes and join to gating run summaries via IDs. In the console we’ll have a “change history” view that shows gating status and links.

[24:26] Priya Desai: Great.

[24:28] Mark Ellison: And do you include “failed gating attempted” as an event too.

[24:33] Kevin Osei: Yes, attempted applies that are blocked are logged as well, with status=blocked and reasons.

[24:41] Priya Desai: Perfect. That prevents someone from trying repeatedly.

[24:46] Miguel Santos: Right.

[24:47] Elena Petrova: Sorry, I keep asking. But what about “config drift” if something changes at runtime. Like a human edits a config directly.

[24:57] Ethan Park: In our model, runtime configs are managed via control plane. Direct edits aren’t supported. If you’re on private and do something out-of-band, we can’t prevent that, but it wouldn’t be considered a supported path. The official path is audited.

[25:14] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[25:16] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[25:18] Miguel Santos: Want to do recap and next steps.

[25:21] Priya Desai: Yes.

[25:22] Miguel Santos: So Redwood will send: sample audit event JSON + schema doc, details on retention defaults and configurable retention, and an overview of RBAC and override approvals. Acme will send SIEM requirements and retention requirements. Then we schedule a follow-up, maybe 30 minutes.

[25:44] Priya Desai: Good. Also include your SOC 2 report process and a statement on prompt/output retention for evals.

[25:51] Marcus Lin: Yep, we’ll provide that under NDA.

[25:54] Kevin Osei: And I’ll include notes on field-level redaction and payload size limits.

[26:00] Priya Desai: Great.

[26:02] Jordan Kim: Thanks everyone.

[26:04] Miguel Santos: Thanks.

(Recording ended early in transcript export; remainder of call contained scheduling and NDA logistics.)
